name: Flesh Red
lede: Flesh red is a pinkish red from the colour charts of natural history, where Patrick Syme's edition of Werner's nomenclature named human skin, larkspur petals and baryte as its examples; on screens its swatch has aged into a pale peach.

sections.title: A mineralogist's red
sections.body:
Flesh red is number 88 among the reds of *Werner's Nomenclature of Colours*, the chart that Patrick Syme issued in 1814 and enlarged in 1821 [4][5]. Abraham Werner (1749-1817) was a mining-school mineralogist who proposed in 1774 that minerals be described by their visible properties, colour first, and his list ran to 54 colours under eight principal headings [1]. Each colour in Syme's chart came with an animal, a vegetable and a mineral example, so a reader could match a specimen by eye [2].

For flesh red the three were human skin, the larkspur and baryte, also called heavy spar, with limestone as a second mineral [2][4]. Werner's recipe blends rose red with some tile red and a touch of white [2]. Rose red is itself carmine red lightened with plenty of white and a hint of cochineal red [2]. Baty glosses flesh red as pinkish [3]. In Syme's numbering it sits between Arterial Blood Red at 87 and [[rose-red]] at 89 [4].

The name outlived the chart in dictionaries. Paterson still defines flesh-red as a red often used to describe minerals and crystals, while plain *flesh* there means a moderate pink [6].

sections.title: The swatch is paler than the name
sections.body:
The swatch on this page, #E9C49D, comes from a scan of an aged Werner chart, so it is approximate [8]. Read by the ISCC-NBS method it is a pale orange yellow, nowhere near a pink [8]. Its nearest named neighbor is [[peach]], 5.0 CIEDE2000 units away [8]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary lists two look-alikes, Crea, first recorded in 1590, and Peach Blow, first recorded in 1861 [8].

Treat flesh red as Syme's pinkish red, and the swatch as what paper and light have done to it since [8]. Anyone matching a flower to the chart today would have to remember that the paper has moved.

sections.title: A word that assumed one skin
sections.body:
Werner's animal example, human skin, belongs to a longer and less comfortable history. In the tenth edition of his *Systema naturae* (1758-59), Linnaeus used skin colour as the first term for describing the human varieties, and Baty notes the shadow this cast over anthropology and biology [3]. The chart then turned that example into a single patch.

St Clair points out that *flesh* and *nude*, as colour words, presuppose a pale skin tone [7]. The colour became popular for women's underthings in the 1920s and 1930s, and Paterson dates *flesh-coloured* to pink silk stockings of the 1920s [6][7]. Crayola renamed its flesh crayon peach in 1962 [7].

Earlier craftspeople used the word more literally. The twelfth-century monk Theophilus advised glaziers that a pot of glass which had turned tawny should be used for flesh colour, as Finlay quotes him [11].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch fills at least five per cent of the canvas in 813 works, or 3.4 per cent [9]. The rate is far higher in South Asian painting: 77 of 721 Indian works carry it, 3.1 times the archive rate, including 22 of 96 Kalighat paintings and 25 of 168 Mughal ones [9]. Among individual painters, [[painter:xugu|Xugu]] carries it in 9 of his 16 works [9].

It is almost always a light. About 95 per cent of its area plays highlight rather than shadow, which fits a color that is often the paper or silk itself [9]. The picture where it covers the most canvas is the thirteenth-century [[painting:cma-149391|White-Robed Guanyin]], at 98 per cent, and an Indian court portrait, [[painting:cma-153531|Maharaja Rai Singh of Bikaner]], follows at 89 per cent [9]. The decade with the highest rate is the 1710s, with 13 of 169 paintings [9]. In the same paintings it keeps company with [[tan]], [[beige]] and [[ecru]], each far more often than chance would suggest [9].

In Google Books, *flesh red* peaks around 1808, stands at 44 per cent of that peak by 1900 and at 2 per cent by 2000 [10]. All archive figures are photographs of aged, varnished paintings and silks, so a color match is not a pigment test [9].

questions.q: Which human feature did Syme's chart give as the animal example for flesh red?
Why does the Flesh Red swatch on this page read as a pale peach rather than a pink?
choices: It comes from an aged chart, so it is approximate and paler than the name suggests
Syme chose a peach for the name
Pink is not a color in the Werner system
questions.answer: It comes from an aged chart, so it is approximate and paler than the name suggests

questions.q: In what year did Crayola rename its flesh crayon peach?

openers: Flesh red was a mineralogist's term: no. 88 in Werner's reds, with human skin, larkspur and baryte as its three examples.
Crayola renamed its flesh crayon peach in 1962; the Werner chart's flesh red had already aged into peach long before.
Look at Indian and Chinese painting on silk or paper: this color is often the ground itself, found in 3.1 times as many Indian works as the archive average.
